summary: For 9–10 year olds comparing animal life cycles across mammals, birds, amphibians and insects, and drawing the contrast between metamorphosis (a change of body FORM during the cycle) and direct development (young are smaller versions of the adult and grow gradually). Within metamorphosis, distinguish complete (butterfly, via a pupa) from incomplete (grasshopper, gradual via nymph stages, no pupa); amphibians also metamorphose, while birds and mammals show direct development. The central teaching move is side-by-side comparison so the contrast emerges, anchored to vivid exemplars (frog, butterfly, grasshopper, robin/chick, dog/kitten) and returning to the universal stages (birth/hatching, growth, reproduction, death) shared by all cycles. Primary activity: assemble and run cycles to observe transformation versus growth; supported by labelled diagrams, a conversational extension, and assessment of ordering and classification.
misconceptions: Thinking metamorphosis just means 'getting bigger' rather than a complete change of body form.
Believing all insects undergo the same (complete) metamorphosis, missing that grasshoppers/dragonflies develop gradually (incomplete).
Assuming a tadpole and a frog, or a caterpillar and a butterfly, are different animals rather than stages of one life cycle.
Thinking mammals and birds also metamorphose because they change as they grow, not distinguishing growth from change of form.

activities.title: Build and run four life cycles side by side
steps: Arrange the stages of each cycle in correct order into a ring: mammal (born live → grows → adult, no change of form); bird (egg → chick → adult); amphibian (egg → tadpole → frog); insect complete (egg → larva/caterpillar → pupa → adult butterfly); insect incomplete (egg → nymph → adult grasshopper).

Run two cycles at once and watch each transition: the tadpole sprouting legs and losing its tail to become a frog; the caterpillar shedding its skin to form a pupa (chrysalis) and later emerging as a butterfly; the grasshopper nymph moulting through stages that already resemble the adult while gradually developing (wing buds growing into wings), with no pupa; the chick and the puppy simply getting bigger with the same basic body form.
Compare the butterfly cycle directly beside the grasshopper cycle and describe in your own words how a complete transformation through a pupa differs from gradual change through nymph stages.

Tag each completed cycle — metamorphosis (complete, like the butterfly through a pupa; or incomplete, like the grasshopper through nymph stages; the amphibian also metamorphoses) versus direct development (bird, mammal) — and justify the tag by pointing to what you observed changing (or not changing) in body form and whether a pupa stage is present.
activities.insight: Metamorphosis is a change of body FORM within one individual's life cycle (not merely getting bigger). In complete metamorphosis (butterfly) the change is dramatic and passes through a pupa; in incomplete metamorphosis (grasshopper) the change is gradual through nymph stages that already resemble the adult, with no pupa — but both are metamorphosis. Amphibians also metamorphose. Birds and mammals show direct development: the young already resembles the adult and simply grows larger with no larval or nymph stage.

activities.title: Explore labelled cycle diagrams and compare
steps: Study labelled circular life-cycle diagrams for a mammal, bird, amphibian and insect; for each stage, uncover or note what happens at that point in the cycle.
Overlay or place two cycles next to each other and highlight exactly where one cycle changes body form and the other does not.
Trace the shared ring of universal stages — birth/hatching, growth, reproduction, death — underneath every cycle to see diversity within a common frame.
activities.insight: The canonical cycle diagram makes the stages and their order explicit and names the vocabulary, while a compare view localises where metamorphosis differs from direct development; all cycles share the same universal stages.

activities.title: Classify and sequence cycles
steps: Put the stages of each cycle in order, including the butterfly (egg → larva → pupa → adult).

Sort the example animals into 'undergoes metamorphosis' (amphibians such as the frog; insects such as the butterfly and grasshopper) versus 'direct development' (birds, mammals), and explain the sorting rule.

Match each group to its cycle type and distinguish complete metamorphosis (egg→larva→pupa→adult) from incomplete (egg→nymph→adult), using the presence or absence of a pupa as the tell — remembering that incomplete metamorphosis is still metamorphosis.
Answer: a chick hatches looking like a small fluffy version of the adult — is that metamorphosis or direct development, and why?
activities.insight: Learners can both order the stages and classify each group by the change-of-form criterion, distinguishing complete from incomplete metamorphosis while keeping both on the metamorphosis side, and separating these from the direct development of birds and mammals.

activities.title: Talk it through: same creature or different animal?
steps: Discuss: 'A caterpillar turns into a butterfly. Is that butterfly the SAME creature the caterpillar was, or a different animal?' and give your reasons.
Discuss: 'Does a kitten change in that same big way as it grows into a cat — why or why not?'

Respond to probes: What happens inside the chrysalis — does the caterpillar keep its caterpillar body? Is a tadpole a baby fish or a baby frog, and how can you tell? Name an animal group that does NOT go through metamorphosis and say how its young grow instead.
Explain how you can tell whether an insect transforms completely (through a pupa) or changes gradually (through nymph stages), using the butterfly and grasshopper as examples.
activities.insight: Inside the pupa (chrysalis), a single individual's caterpillar body is reorganised into the adult butterfly — it is the same animal, not a replacement — which is a complete change of form; a kitten growing into a cat keeps the same body form and just gets bigger (direct development). A tadpole is a young frog, not a fish.

checkQuestion: Say: 'A caterpillar turns into a butterfly. Is that butterfly the SAME creature the caterpillar was, or a different animal? And does a kitten change in that same big way as it grows into a cat — why, or why not?'
checkAnswer: The butterfly is the SAME individual — inside the chrysalis the caterpillar's own body is reorganised into the butterfly; it doesn't die and get replaced. A kitten does NOT change like that: it grows by direct development, keeping the same basic body form and just getting bigger. Insects and amphibians undergo metamorphosis (a complete change of body form); mammals and birds do not.
